To check that a particular decomposition of a fraction is valid, we need to check the following:

Content:
- All denominators in the decomposition must equal the denominator of the fraction.
- The sum of numerators of the decomposition must equal the numerator of the fraction.

items.title: Identifying Decompositions of a Given Fraction

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following are decompositions of the fraction [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}?]

  1. [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}]

  2. [MATH: \dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{4}{10}]

  3. [MATH: \dfrac{4}{11}+\dfrac{3}{11}]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following are decompositions of the fraction [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}?]

1. [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}]
2. [MATH: \dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{4}{10}]
3. [MATH: \dfrac{4}{11}+\dfrac{3}{11}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine each expression in turn.

  • I is a decomposition of [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}.] Indeed,

    • each fraction in the expression has a denominator of [MATH: 10,] and

    • the sum of numerators is [MATH: 7.] [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{1+1+2+3}{10} = \dfrac{7}{10}]

  • II is not a decomposition of [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}.] Indeed,

    • each fraction in the expression has a denominator of [MATH: 10,] but

    • the sum of numerators is [MATH: 9.] [MATH: \dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{2+3+4}{10} = \dfrac{9}{10}]

  • III is not a decomposition of [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}.] Notice that each fraction in the expression has a denominator of [MATH: 11.]

    As a result, this cannot be a decomposition of a fraction with a denominator of [MATH: 10.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Content:
How can we find a fraction decomposition of the mixed number [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7}?]

Content:
First, recall that [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7}] can be viewed as the sum of its whole and fractional parts:

Content:
[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7} = 2 + \dfrac{3}{7}]

Content:
In turn, the whole number [MATH: 2] can be written as

Content:
[MATH: 2 = 1 + 1 = \dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{7}{7}.]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7} =
\underbrace{\dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{7}{7}}_{\large 2} +
\dfrac{3}{7}]

Content:
which is a fraction decomposition of [MATH: 2\,\dfrac37.]

Content:
Now, adding these fractions to make a mixed number, we get

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{17}{7}.]

Content:
Therefore, we can make more decompositions of [MATH: 2\,\dfrac37] by adding together fractions whose denominator is [MATH: 7] and whose numerators add to [MATH: 17.] For example,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{5}{7} + \dfrac{9}{7} + \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{17}{7}.]

Which of the following fractions gives a true statement when inserted into the blank space?

  3. [MATH: \dfrac{4}{6}]

3. [MATH: \dfrac{4}{6}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, recall that [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] can be viewed as the sum of the whole and fractional parts:

[MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4} = 3 + \dfrac{1}{4}]

In turn, the whole number [MATH: 3] can be written as

[MATH: 3 = 1 + 1 + 1= \dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4}.]

So, we have

[MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4} = \underbrace{\dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4}}_{\large 3} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{4+4+4+1}{4} = \dfrac{\color{blue}13}{4}.]

As a result, any decomposition of [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] must contain fractions

  • whose denominator is [MATH: 4,] and

  • the sum of all numerators gives [MATH: {\color{blue}13}.]

Among the given options, the only fraction with these properties is [MATH: \dfrac{5}{4}.] Indeed, its denominator is [MATH: 4] and

[MATH: \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1px solid black]{\dfrac{5}{4}} + \dfrac{2}{4} + \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{5+2+6}{4} = \dfrac{\color{blue}13}{4}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To determine the missing fraction, we first decompose [MATH: \dfrac67] into the sum of [MATH: 6] instances of [MATH: \dfrac17{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 6]

Content:
Examining the known fractions on the left-hand side of the given equation, from left to right, we have the following:

Content:
- To get [MATH: \color{blue}\dfrac{1}{7},] we need [MATH: 1] instance of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{7}]
- To get [MATH: \color{red}\dfrac{2}{7},] we need [MATH: 2] instances of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{7}]

Content:
Let's add these to our diagram:

Content:
[MATH: 6]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: 6]

Content:
Therefore, we obtain the decomposition

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{7}} + \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1px solid black]{\color{violet}\dfrac{3}{7}} + {\color{red}\dfrac{2}{7}} = \dfrac{6}{7}.]

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Missing Fraction in a Decomposition

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, recall that [MATH: \dfrac{9}{10}] can be viewed as the sum of [MATH: 9] instances of the fraction [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}{:}]

[MATH: 9]

Examining the known fractions on the left-hand side of the given equation, from left to right, we have the following:

- [MATH: 2] instances of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}] gives the fraction [MATH: \color{blue}\dfrac{2}{10}]
- [MATH: 4] instances of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}] gives the fraction [MATH: \color{red}\dfrac{4}{10}]

Let's add these to our diagram:

[MATH: 9]

We have [MATH: 3] instances of [MATH: \dfrac1{10}] remaining, and these give the fraction [MATH: {\color{violet}{\dfrac3{10}}}.]

[MATH: 9]

This gives the decomposition

[MATH: {\color{blue}\dfrac{2}{10}} + {\color{red}\dfrac{4}{10}}+ \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1px solid black]{\color{violet}\dfrac{3}{10}} = \dfrac{9}{10}.]

Therefore, the missing fraction is [MATH: {\color{violet}{\dfrac3{10}}}.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Properties of Fraction Decomposition

Content:
To check that a particular decomposition of a fraction is valid, we need to check the following:

Content:
- All denominators in the decomposition must equal the denominator of the fraction.
- The sum of numerators of the decomposition must equal the numerator of the fraction.

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Decompositions of a Given Fraction

Example Prompt:
Which of the following are decompositions of the fraction [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}?]

1. [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}]
2. [MATH: \dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{4}{10}]
3. [MATH: \dfrac{4}{11}+\dfrac{3}{11}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine each expression in turn.

- I is a decomposition of [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}.] Indeed,

- each fraction in the expression has a denominator of [MATH: 10,] and
- the sum of numerators is [MATH: 7.]
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{1+1+2+3}{10} = \dfrac{7}{10}]
- II is not a decomposition of [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}.] Indeed,

- each fraction in the expression has a denominator of [MATH: 10,] but
- the sum of numerators is [MATH: 9.]
[MATH: \dfrac{2}{10}+\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{2+3+4}{10} = \dfrac{9}{10}]
- III is not a decomposition of [MATH: \dfrac{7}{10}.] Notice that each fraction in the expression has a denominator of [MATH: 11.]

As a result, this cannot be a decomposition of a fraction with a denominator of [MATH: 10.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Item 9 — Tutorial: Decompositions of Mixed Numbers

Content:
How can we find a fraction decomposition of the mixed number [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7}?]

Content:
First, recall that [MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7}] can be viewed as the sum of its whole and fractional parts:

Content:
[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7} = 2 + \dfrac{3}{7}]

Content:
In turn, the whole number [MATH: 2] can be written as

Content:
[MATH: 2 = 1 + 1 = \dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{7}{7}.]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: 2 \, \dfrac{3}{7} =
\underbrace{\dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{7}{7}}_{\large 2} +
\dfrac{3}{7}]

Content:
which is a fraction decomposition of [MATH: 2\,\dfrac37.]

Content:
Now, adding these fractions to make a mixed number, we get

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{7}{7} + \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{17}{7}.]

Content:
Therefore, we can make more decompositions of [MATH: 2\,\dfrac37] by adding together fractions whose denominator is [MATH: 7] and whose numerators add to [MATH: 17.] For example,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{5}{7} + \dfrac{9}{7} + \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{17}{7}.]

---

Item 10 — Example: Finding a Missing Fraction in a Mixed Number Decomposition

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{\dfrac{a}{a}}} + \dfrac{2}{4} + \dfrac{6}{4} = 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4}]

Which of the following fractions gives a true statement when inserted into the blank space?

1. [MATH: \dfrac{5}{4}]
2. [MATH: \dfrac{3}{4}]
3. [MATH: \dfrac{4}{6}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, recall that [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] can be viewed as the sum of the whole and fractional parts:

[MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4} = 3 + \dfrac{1}{4}]

In turn, the whole number [MATH: 3] can be written as

[MATH: 3 = 1 + 1 + 1= \dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4}.]

So, we have

[MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4} =
\underbrace{\dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4} + \dfrac{4}{4}}_{\large 3} +
\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{4+4+4+1}{4} = \dfrac{\color{blue}13}{4}.]

As a result, any decomposition of [MATH: 3 \, \dfrac{1}{4}] must contain fractions

- whose denominator is [MATH: 4,] and
- the sum of all numerators gives [MATH: {\color{blue}13}.]

Among the given options, the only fraction with these properties is [MATH: \dfrac{5}{4}.] Indeed, its denominator is [MATH: 4] and

[MATH: \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1px solid black]{\dfrac{5}{4}} + \dfrac{2}{4} + \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{5+2+6}{4} = \dfrac{\color{blue}13}{4}.]
